evidence.claim: Part of the journey follows an earlier transportation corridor: the main north-south stage road that is now Oregon Route 31.

evidence.claim: In 1909, a new connecting road linked it to Fremont as the homestead town grew.
evidence.quote: In 1909, a new road was built to connect Fremont with the main north–south stage road, now Oregon Route 31.

evidence.claim: By 1912, a daily stage brought settlers from the Bend railhead.
evidence.quote: By 1912, the local stage line was transporting settlers from the railhead in Bend to Fremont on a daily scheduled basis.

evidence.claim: Drought beginning in 1915 eventually forced homesteaders to abandon farms; Fremont’s post office closed in 1919.
evidence.quote: The drought continued through 1919 and then into the 1920s.  This forced homesteaders to abandon their farms and the town of Fremont quickly followed.  The Fremont post office closed in 1919.

evidence.claim: Fort Rock’s walls began as volcanic material thrown up through a lake bottom.
evidence.quote: Fort Rock was created when basalt magma rose to the surface and encountered the wet muds of a lake bottom.

evidence.claim: Steam drove lava particles and ash into the air; they fell into a ring that stood like an island in the lake.
evidence.quote: Powered by a jet of steam, molten basalt was blown into the air, creating a fountain of hot lava particles and frothy ash. The pieces and blobs of hot lava and ash rained down around the vent and formed a saucer-shaped ring of lapilli tuff and volcanic ash sitting like an island in the lake waters.

evidence.claim: Waves cut terraces into its outer walls, leaving marks of former lake levels above the dry valley floor.
evidence.quote: The wave-cut terraces on the south side of the ring mark former lake levels of this now-dry lakebed.

evidence.claim: Nearby Fort Rock Cave yielded sandals woven from sagebrush bark during excavations led by Luther Cressman.
evidence.quote: Anthropologist Luther Cressman and his team recovered a significant collection of artifacts

evidence.claim: Nearby Fort Rock Cave yielded sandals woven from sagebrush bark during excavations led by Luther Cressman.
evidence.quote: 95 sandals woven from sagebrush bark

evidence.claim: The rock formation is reached by a seven-mile excursion from Route 31.
evidence.quote: Fort Rock State Park is an easy 7 miles off Oregon Route 31

evidence.claim: The name Fort Rock refers to the tall, straight sides, which resemble the palisades of a fort.
evidence.quote: Its name is derived from the tall, straight sides that resemble the palisades of a fort.

evidence.claim: Wave-cut terraces on the south side record former lake levels.
evidence.quote: The wave-cut terraces on the south side of the ring mark former lake levels

evidence.claim: At Valley Falls, Abert Rim rises more than 2,000 feet above the byway, a 30-mile escarpment along the horizon.
evidence.quote: a 30-mile-long fault escarpment one of the nation's longest and most continuous fault escarpments. This rim rises more than 2,000 feet above the Byway.

evidence.claim: The wall records two different processes: basalt lava first covered the region, then faults broke and tilted great blocks of land.
evidence.quote: At that time basaltic flood lavas covered much of eastern Oregon. In subsequent faulting, great blocks were tilted

evidence.claim: A sheer basalt cap finishes the rim.
evidence.quote: finishing with an 820-foot (250 m) sheer-sided basalt cap.

evidence.claim: Lake Abert occupies another block and has no outlet, although the Chewaucan River feeds it from the south.
evidence.quote: while Lake Abert lies on top of another.

evidence.claim: Lake Abert occupies another block and has no outlet, although the Chewaucan River feeds it from the south.
evidence.quote: The Chewaucan River enters Lake Abert from the south, however it has no outlet.

evidence.claim: A byway kiosk just south of Valley Falls explains the rim’s formation.
evidence.quote: Along the highway just south of the Valley Falls, there is an Outback Scenic Byway kiosk that explains how Abert Rim was formed.

evidence.claim: The lake’s highly alkaline water supports brine shrimp, which in turn feed migrating birds along this high-desert corridor.
evidence.quote: The lake's high alkalinity make it ideal habitat for brine shrimp, which provide forage for migrating birds.

evidence.claim: From Valley Falls, the cliff face of Abert Rim is unobstructed.
evidence.quote: From Valley Falls, visitors have an unobstructed view of Abert Rim's cliff face.

evidence.claim: Lakeview calls itself the “Tallest Town in Oregon,” standing in Goose Lake Valley at the foot of the Warner Mountains.
evidence.quote: The city bills itself as the "Tallest Town in Oregon"

evidence.claim: Lakeview calls itself the “Tallest Town in Oregon,” standing in Goose Lake Valley at the foot of the Warner Mountains.
evidence.quote: Lakeview is situated in the Goose Lake Valley at the foot of the Warner Mountains

evidence.claim: Its downtown was largely remade after a fire destroyed 64 buildings in May 1900.
evidence.quote: On May 22, 1900, a fire burned most of Lakeview.  There were no deaths, but 64 buildings were destroyed.

evidence.claim: The Lake County Examiner salvaged enough equipment to publish the next day, and most of the town had been rebuilt by October.
evidence.quote: the staff of the Lake County Examiner newspaper rescued enough equipment and material to publish a special edition the day after the fire.  Most of the town was rebuilt by October of that year.

evidence.claim: Financing and leadership from Bernard Daly helped that recovery.
evidence.quote: The town's rapid recovery was due in large part to the financing and leadership provided by Bernard Daly.

evidence.claim: A narrow-gauge railway reached Lakeview from Reno in 1911; its later conversion to standard gauge encouraged sawmills to open and broadened the town’s economy.
evidence.quote: In 1911, a narrow-gauge railway connected Lakeview with Reno, Nevada.

evidence.claim: A narrow-gauge railway reached Lakeview from Reno in 1911; its later conversion to standard gauge encouraged sawmills to open and broadened the town’s economy.
evidence.quote: Southern Pacific converted the track to standard gauge.  The new standard rail connection prompted several sawmills to operate in Lakeview, expanding the town's economic base.

flags: Cache does not establish the modern byway’s construction or designation chronology. History is limited to the documented stage-road corridor and Fremont connection, not an assertion that the entire byway follows that road.
Dropped the current 13,000-year age for sagebrush sandals: Fort Rock Cave lead gives that range, but its body assigns the debated 13,000 BP date to charcoal. No artifact age used.
Fort Rock height differs between ODOT (325 feet) and Wikipedia (about 200 feet); omitted.

Lakeview elevation varies within Wikipedia (4,757 and 4,800 feet); retained only the attributed town nickname. Geyser timing omitted because ODOT says generally, while Wikipedia documents periods of dormancy without a resolved cause.
